name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q01 - Polarity of capacitor plates during magnetic approach

questiontext.text:
As shown in the schematic diagram, a circular conducting loop containing an open capacitor with parallel plates labeled Plate A and Plate B is positioned vertically. Two identical bar magnets are pushed simultaneously along the horizontal central axis towards the loop with identical speeds:

The magnet on the left approaches with its North pole facing the loop, while the magnet on the right approaches with its South pole facing the loop. In this situation, the polarities acquired by Plate A and Plate B of the capacitor are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A conducting wire loop is oriented vertically and interrupted by a capacitor with an upper plate labeled Plate A and a lower plate labeled Plate B.
A bar magnet on the left approaches the loop with its North pole moving towards the loop.
A bar magnet on the right approaches the loop with its South pole moving towards the loop.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
View the loop along the common axis from the left side.
According to Lenz's law, an induced electromotive force produces an electric current whose magnetic effect opposes the change in magnetic flux that creates it.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Lenz's Law: The direction of the induced current opposes the motion of the magnetic poles causing the flux change.
An approaching North pole induces a North magnetic polarity on the facing side of the coil (corresponding to a counter-clockwise current when viewed from that side).
An approaching South pole induces a South magnetic polarity on the facing side of the coil (corresponding to a clockwise current when viewed from that side).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Effect of the left magnet: The North pole moves to the right towards the left face of the loop. To oppose the approach of this North pole, the left face of the loop must develop North polarity. Viewed from the left, a North pole corresponds to a counter-clockwise induced current.
2. Effect of the right magnet: The South pole moves to the left towards the right face of the loop. To oppose the approach of this South pole, the right face of the loop must develop South polarity. Viewed from the right side, a South polarity corresponds to a clockwise current. When this clockwise current on the right face is viewed from the left side, it is also directed counter-clockwise.
3. Combined effect: Both approaching magnets reinforce each other, inducing a net counter-clockwise current in the wire loop as observed from the left side.
4. Charge accumulation on the capacitor: Because the circuit contains an open capacitor gap, electric current cannot cross the dielectric. Looking from the left, a counter-clockwise circulating tendency causes positive charge to flow upwards along the right segment of the loop and deposit onto Plate A, while negative charge accumulates on Plate B (or electrons are displaced from Plate A toward Plate B). Consequently, Plate A becomes positively charged and Plate B becomes negatively charged.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The polarity of Plate A is positive with respect to Plate B, which conforms fully to energy conservation and Lenz's law. Therefore, Plate A is positive and Plate B is negative.

answer.text: Plate A is positive and Plate B is negative.
Plate A is negative and Plate B is positive.
Both Plate A and Plate B acquire positive charge.
Both Plate A and Plate B remain uncharged as the induced effects cancel each other.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q02 - Motional electromotive force on sliding conductor

questiontext.text:
A straight conducting rod PQ of length \(l = 0.40\text{ m}\) and internal resistance \(r = 0.20\,\Omega\) slides smoothly on two parallel frictionless horizontal rails separated by \(0.40\text{ m}\). A fixed resistor \(R = 0.60\,\Omega\) is connected between the ends of the rails, forming a closed rectangular loop, as shown in the figure:

A uniform vertical magnetic field \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\) acts perpendicular to the plane of the rails, directed into the page. If the rod PQ is pulled to the left with a constant velocity \(v = 6.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\), what are the magnitude of the induced current in the loop and the magnitude and direction of the external horizontal force required to maintain the steady motion of the rod?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of the moving rod: \(l = 0.40\text{ m}\)
Internal resistance of the rod: \(r = 0.20\,\Omega\)
External resistance of the rail circuit: \(R = 0.60\,\Omega\)
Uniform magnetic field: \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\), directed perpendicular into the plane
Velocity of the rod: \(v = 6.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) to the left

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The conducting rails have negligible electrical resistance and friction is absent.
The rod maintains continuous electrical contact with the rails while moving at constant velocity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Motional electromotive force induced across a conductor moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field: \[\varepsilon = B l v\] 2. Total circuit resistance: \[R_{\text{total}} = R + r\] 3. Induced electric current: \[I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R_{\text{total}}}\] 4. Magnetic braking force on the current-carrying conductor: \[F_m = I l B\] 5. For steady motion at constant velocity, the net force must be zero, so the external applied force must balance the magnetic force: \[F_{\text{ext}} = F_m\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate the induced electromotive force: \[\varepsilon = (0.50\text{ T}) \times (0.40\text{ m}) \times (6.0\text{ m s}^{-1}) = 1.20\text{ V}\] 2. Calculate the total resistance of the loop: \[R_{\text{total}} = 0.60\,\Omega + 0.20\,\Omega = 0.80\,\Omega\] 3. Calculate the magnitude of the induced current: \[I = \frac{1.20\text{ V}}{0.80\,\Omega} = 1.50\text{ A}\] 4. Direction of induced current: As the rod moves to the left, the enclosed area of the loop decreases, causing the inward magnetic flux to decrease. By Lenz's law, the induced current must create an inward magnetic field to oppose this decrease. Using the right-hand rule, an inward field requires a clockwise current around the loop. Thus, through the rod PQ, current flows downwards from P to Q.
5. Calculate the magnetic force acting on the rod: \[F_m = I l B = (1.50\text{ A}) \times (0.40\text{ m}) \times (0.50\text{ T}) = 0.30\text{ N}\] By the magnetic force relation \(\mathbf{F} = I(\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{B})\), with current directed downwards from P to Q and magnetic field into the page, the magnetic force opposes the motion and acts to the right.
6. External force required: To maintain a constant velocity of \(6.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) to the left, the external applied force must oppose the magnetic braking force and act in the direction of motion: \[F_{\text{ext}} = 0.30\text{ N} \text{ directed to the left}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensional units: \(\text{V}/\Omega = \text{A}\) and \(\text{A} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{T} = \text{N}\), which are fully consistent.
Mechanical power supplied \(P_{\text{mech}} = F_{\text{ext}} v = 0.30 \times 6.0 = 1.80\text{ W}\) equals the electrical power dissipated \(P_{\text{elec}} = I^2 R_{\text{total}} = (1.50)^2 \times 0.80 = 2.25 \times 0.80 = 1.80\text{ W}\). Energy is strictly conserved.
The final answer is \(1.50\text{ A}\) and \(0.30\text{ N}\) directed to the left.

answer.text: \(1.50\text{ A}\) and \(0.30\text{ N}\) directed to the left
\(1.50\text{ A}\) and \(0.30\text{ N}\) directed to the right
\(2.00\text{ A}\) and \(0.40\text{ N}\) directed to the left
\(1.20\text{ A}\) and \(0.24\text{ N}\) directed to the right

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q03 - Electromotive force induced in rotating spokes

questiontext.text:
A metallic wheel consisting of 12 identical radial spokes, each of length \(R = 0.50\text{ m}\), is rotated at a constant angular speed \(\omega = 20\text{ rad s}^{-1}\) about its central axle in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \(B = 0.80\text{ T}\), as shown in the diagram:

The outer ends of all spokes are electrically connected by a conducting circular rim. What is the magnitude of the induced electromotive force between the central axle and the outer rim, and how does this electromotive force change if the number of spokes is doubled to 24?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of spokes: \(N_{\text{spokes}} = 12\)
Length of each spoke (radius of wheel): \(R = 0.50\text{ m}\)
Angular velocity of rotation: \(\omega = 20\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Uniform magnetic field: \(B = 0.80\text{ T}\) perpendicular to the wheel plane

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The spokes are identical radial conductors rotating in a steady, uniform magnetic field.
The central axle acts as one common terminal and the continuous conducting rim acts as the other terminal.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Electromotive force induced across a rotating conductor of length \(R\) pivoting at one end about an axis parallel to a uniform magnetic field: \[\varepsilon = \int_0^R B v \,\mathrm{d}r = \int_0^R B (\omega r) \,\mathrm{d}r = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2\] 2. Circuit configuration: All radial spokes share the same central axle at one end and the same metallic rim at the other end. Therefore, each spoke acts as an identical source of electromotive force connected in parallel.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Compute the electromotive force induced across an individual rotating spoke: \[\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.80\text{ T}) \times (20\text{ rad s}^{-1}) \times (0.50\text{ m})^2\] \[\varepsilon = 0.40 \times 20 \times 0.25\text{ V} = 2.0\text{ V}\] 2. Parallel combination analysis: In any parallel combination of identical cells or electromotive force sources with equal potential differences across common terminals, the overall potential difference across the terminals equals the potential difference of a single branch, regardless of the number of parallel branches.
3. Effect of doubling the number of spokes to 24: Adding more spokes simply places additional identical sources of electromotive force \(\varepsilon = 2.0\text{ V}\) in parallel. The terminal potential difference between the axle and the rim remains unchanged at \(2.0\text{ V}\) (while internal resistance decreases, the open-circuit induced electromotive force is strictly unaltered).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \(\text{T} \cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^2 = (\text{N} \cdot \text{s} / (\text{A} \cdot \text{m})) \cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^2 = \text{N} \cdot \text{m} / \text{A} = \text{J} / \text{C} = \text{V}\). The units are verified.
The induced electromotive force is \(2.0\text{ V}\), and it remains unchanged when the number of spokes is doubled.

answer.text: \(2.0\text{ V}\), and the induced electromotive force remains unchanged.
\(2.0\text{ V}\), and the induced electromotive force doubles to \(4.0\text{ V}\).
\(4.0\text{ V}\), and the induced electromotive force remains unchanged.
\(24.0\text{ V}\), and the induced electromotive force halves to \(1.0\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q04 - Induced electromotive force in moving rectangular loop

questiontext.text:
A planar rectangular conducting wire loop has a length \(L = 0.20\text{ m}\) parallel to the direction of motion and a width \(w = 0.10\text{ m}\) perpendicular to the motion. The loop moves horizontally at a constant speed \(v = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) into, through, and out of a bounded region of uniform magnetic field \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\) directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop into the page:

The width of the magnetic field region is \(d = 0.50\text{ m}\). What is the induced electromotive force \(\varepsilon\) and the sense of the induced current when:

(i) the loop is entering the magnetic field region, and
(ii) the loop is completely inside the magnetic field region?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Width of the loop (perpendicular to velocity): \(w = 0.10\text{ m}\)
Length of the loop (parallel to velocity): \(L = 0.20\text{ m}\)
Constant velocity: \(v = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Magnetic field: \(B = 0.50\text{ T}\), oriented perpendicular into the plane
Width of field region: \(d = 0.50\text{ m}\) (noting \(d > L\))

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field is strictly uniform inside the boundary and drops sharply to zero outside.
The orientation of the loop remains fixed throughout the motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction: \[\varepsilon = -\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\] where magnetic flux is \(\Phi_{\mathrm{B}} = B A_{\text{enclosed}}\).
2. Rate of change of enclosed area while entering: \[\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = w v\] 3. Lenz's Law: The direction of the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes any change in the existing magnetic flux.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Entering the field: As the front edge enters, the area inside the magnetic field increases at the rate: \[\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = w v = (0.10\text{ m}) \times (2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}) = 0.20\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-1}\] The rate of change of magnetic flux is: \[\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = B \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = (0.50\text{ T}) \times (0.20\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-1}) = 0.10\text{ V}\] Thus, the magnitude of the induced electromotive force is \(\varepsilon = 0.10\text{ V}\).
Direction of current: The magnetic flux directed into the page is increasing. To oppose this increase, the induced current must generate a magnetic field pointing out of the page. By the right-hand grip rule, an out-of-page magnetic field is produced by a counter-clockwise current.
2. Completely inside the field: Because the field region width \(d = 0.50\text{ m}\) exceeds the length of the loop \(L = 0.20\text{ m}\), there is a time interval where the loop is entirely immersed in the uniform field. In this interval, the enclosed area is constant at \(A = w L = 0.02\text{ m}^2\), so the enclosed magnetic flux \(\Phi_{\mathrm{B}} = B w L\) is constant in time: \[\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \implies \varepsilon = 0\text{ V}\] With zero induced electromotive force, no induced current flows through the loop.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units check: \(\text{T} \cdot \text{m} \cdot \text{m s}^{-1} = \text{V}\). Physical behavior matches Faraday's principle: current only exists during the transition when flux is changing.
Therefore, the induced electromotive force is \(0.10\text{ V}\) with counter-clockwise current while entering, and \(0\text{ V}\) with no current while completely inside.

answer.text: \(0.10\text{ V}\) with counter-clockwise current; and \(0\text{ V}\) with no current
\(0.10\text{ V}\) with clockwise current; and \(0.10\text{ V}\) with clockwise current
\(0.20\text{ V}\) with counter-clockwise current; and \(0\text{ V}\) with no current
\(0.10\text{ V}\) with clockwise current; and \(0\text{ V}\) with no current

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q05 - Peak and instantaneous voltage of alternating generator

questiontext.text:
An alternating current generator has a flat armature coil of \(N = 200\) turns, each having an effective cross-sectional area \(A = 0.05\text{ m}^2\). The coil rotates at a constant angular frequency \(\omega = 50\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\) about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \(B = 0.20\text{ T}\). The generated alternating electromotive force as a function of time \(t\) is shown below:

At time \(t = 0\), the plane of the armature coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field lines. What are the peak electromotive force \(\varepsilon_0\) and the instantaneous electromotive force developed across the generator terminals at time \(t = \frac{1}{300}\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of turns in the coil: \(N = 200\)
Area of each turn: \(A = 0.05\text{ m}^2\)
Angular frequency: \(\omega = 50\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Uniform magnetic field strength: \(B = 0.20\text{ T}\)
Initial condition: At \(t = 0\), the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field lines (the angle between the area vector \(\mathbf{A}\) and magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) is \(\theta = 0\)).
Target instant: \(t = \frac{1}{300}\text{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The rotation rate is strictly uniform.
The angle of rotation at any time \(t\) is \(\theta(t) = \omega t\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Magnetic flux linked with the coil of \(N\) turns at time \(t\): \[\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}(t) = N B A \cos(\omega t)\] 2. Instantaneous induced electromotive force via Faraday's Law: \[\varepsilon(t) = -\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = -N B A \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}[\cos(\omega t)] = N B A \omega \sin(\omega t)\] 3. Peak electromotive force occurs when \(\sin(\omega t) = 1\): \[\varepsilon_0 = N B A \omega\] Therefore, \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0 \sin(\omega t)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Compute the peak electromotive force \(\varepsilon_0\): \[\varepsilon_0 = N \times B \times A \times \omega\] \[\varepsilon_0 = 200 \times 0.20\text{ T} \times 0.05\text{ m}^2 \times 50\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\] Notice that \(200 \times 0.05 = 10\). \[\varepsilon_0 = 10 \times 0.20 \times 50\pi = 2.0 \times 50\pi = 100\pi\text{ V}\] 2. Evaluate the argument \(\omega t\) at the given instant \(t = \frac{1}{300}\text{ s}\): \[\omega t = (50\pi) \times \left(\frac{1}{300}\right) = \frac{50\pi}{300} = \frac{\pi}{6}\text{ rad} = 30^\circ\] 3. Determine the instantaneous electromotive force at this instant: \[\varepsilon\left(\frac{1}{300}\text{ s}\right) = \varepsilon_0 \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = (100\pi\text{ V}) \times \frac{1}{2} = 50\pi\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Evaluating numerically: \(\varepsilon_0 = 100\pi \approx 314.2\text{ V}\) and \(\varepsilon = 50\pi \approx 157.1\text{ V}\).
Since the sinusoidal function rises from zero at \(t = 0\) and reaches its maximum at \(t = T/4 = \frac{2\pi}{4\omega} = \frac{1}{100}\text{ s}\), the instant \(t = \frac{1}{300}\text{ s} = T/12\) corresponds exactly to \(30^\circ\), where \(\sin(30^\circ) = 0.5\). The values are physically and mathematically verified.
The peak electromotive force is \(100\pi\text{ V}\) and the instantaneous electromotive force is \(50\pi\text{ V}\).

answer.text: \(100\pi\text{ V}\) and \(50\pi\text{ V}\)
\(100\pi\text{ V}\) and \(50\sqrt{3}\pi\text{ V}\)
\(200\pi\text{ V}\) and \(100\pi\text{ V}\)
\(50\pi\text{ V}\) and \(25\pi\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q06 - Mutual induction between solenoid and coaxial loop

questiontext.text:
A long air-core solenoid has \(n = 2000\text{ turns per meter}\) and a cross-sectional radius \(r_1 = 0.04\text{ m}\). Coaxially positioned near the longitudinal center of the solenoid is a small circular conducting loop of radius \(r_2 = 0.02\text{ m}\) oriented with its plane normal to the axis of the solenoid, as depicted below:

The current in the solenoid is increased at a steady rate from \(1.0\text{ A}\) to \(5.0\text{ A}\) over a time interval of \(0.20\text{ s}\). Given the permeability of free space \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\), what is the magnitude of the electromotive force induced in the small coaxial loop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of turns per unit length of solenoid: \(n = 2000\text{ m}^{-1}\)
Radius of the solenoid: \(r_1 = 0.04\text{ m}\)
Radius of the small circular loop: \(r_2 = 0.02\text{ m}\) (satisfying \(r_2 < r_1\))
Initial solenoid current: \(I_i = 1.0\text{ A}\)
Final solenoid current: \(I_f = 5.0\text{ A}\)
Time interval for current change: \(\Delta t = 0.20\text{ s}\)
Magnetic permeability of free space: \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because the solenoid is long and the small loop is near the center, edge effects are negligible, and the magnetic field inside the solenoid is uniform and parallel to the axis.
The small loop is completely immersed within the solenoid's interior magnetic field.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid carrying current \(I\): \[B = \mu_0 n I\] 2. The magnetic flux linked with the small loop depends on the area of the small loop \(A_2 = \pi r_2^2\) because the magnetic field is uniform across this area: \[\Phi_{\mathrm{B}} = B A_2 = (\mu_0 n I)(\pi r_2^2)\] 3. By Faraday's Law, the magnitude of the induced electromotive force in the loop is: \[\varepsilon = \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mu_0 n (\pi r_2^2) \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Compute the time rate of change of the solenoid current: \[\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{I_f - I_i}{\Delta t} = \frac{5.0\text{ A} - 1.0\text{ A}}{0.20\text{ s}} = \frac{4.0\text{ A}}{0.20\text{ s}} = 20\text{ A s}^{-1}\] 2. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the small loop: \[A_2 = \pi r_2^2 = \pi \times (0.02\text{ m})^2 = 4\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2\] 3. Calculate the rate of change of magnetic field inside the solenoid: \[\frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mu_0 n \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = (4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}) \times (2000\text{ m}^{-1}) \times (20\text{ A s}^{-1})\] \[\frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 40000 = 1.6\pi \times 10^{-2}\text{ T s}^{-1}\] 4. Calculate the induced electromotive force in the loop: \[\varepsilon = A_2 \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = (4\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2) \times (1.6\pi \times 10^{-2}\text{ T s}^{-1})\] \[\varepsilon = 6.4\pi^2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Using the approximation \(\pi^2 \approx 9.87\): \[\varepsilon \approx 6.4 \times 9.87 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V} \approx 6.32 \times 10^{-5}\text{ V} = 63.2\,\mu\text{V}\] Notice that using the outer solenoid radius \(r_1 = 0.04\text{ m}\) instead of the loop radius would erroneously multiply the area by 4, yielding \(25.6\pi^2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V}\). Since only the area bounded by the small loop captures the linked flux, the calculation using \(r_2\) is exact.
The induced electromotive force in the loop is \(6.4\pi^2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V}\).
